choices.text: Every molecule moves faster than it did at 300 K
The average kinetic energy halves, because the speeds spread out
The average kinetic energy doubles, but the speeds stay spread out and some molecules are still slow
Every molecule ends up moving at exactly the same new speed

questions.explanation: Heating doubles the kelvin temperature, so the average kinetic energy (3/2) k T doubles. The trap claim is: In a hotter gas every molecule moves faster. In fact the speeds form a spread at any temperature: the whole spread shifts up, so the average rises, but some molecules are still slow and a few are far faster than the average.
questions.misconception: In a hotter gas every molecule moves faster.
questions.prompt: A gas is heated from 300 K to 600 K at fixed volume. Which statement about its molecules is correct?

choices.text: 1.0 x 10^5 Pa - pressure does not depend on temperature

questions.explanation: At fixed volume and fixed amount of gas, p is proportional to the kelvin temperature T. Doubling T from 300 K to 600 K doubles the pressure: 2.0 x 10^5 Pa. Faster average molecular collisions hit the walls harder and more often.
questions.prompt: A sealed rigid container of gas sits at 300 K with pressure 1.0 x 10^5 Pa. It is heated to 600 K. What is the new pressure?

questions.answer: Atoms at the hot end vibrate with larger amplitude and collide with their neighbours, passing kinetic energy along atom by atom through the lattice; in a metal, free electrons also carry energy rapidly through the rod. No atoms travel the length of the rod - the energy is relayed, and the far end warms as its atoms gain kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: This is conduction: energy transfer by particle collisions (and, in metals, by free electrons) without any bulk movement of the material. The key phrases are vibrate, collide with neighbours, and pass the energy on.
questions.prompt: One end of a metal rod is held in a flame. A minute later the far end feels warm. Explain, at the particle level, how the energy got there.

questions.explanation: Use the ideal-gas law pV = nRT with the temperature in kelvin. Multiply n, R and T first (1246.5), then divide by the volume in cubic metres. The common slip is leaving the volume in litres or the temperature in degrees Celsius.
questions.prompt: An ideal gas of 0.50 mol is held in a container of volume 0.012 m^3 at 300 K. Calculate its pressure. (R = 8.31 J mol^-1 K^-1)

questions.explanation: Radiated power follows the Stefan-Boltzmann law, P = sigma A T^4, so power is proportional to the fourth power of the kelvin temperature. Doubling T multiplies the power by 2^4 = 16.
questions.prompt: A black body is heated so its kelvin temperature doubles. By what factor does its radiated power increase?
